name: Two White Eagles

intro.lead: Six stops round the middle of Saint-Antonin-Noble-Val.
intro.body:
Under a kilometre of walking, about an hour. Three stops ask a question you can only answer by looking at the thing in front of you. Three just need you standing in the right place.

All outdoors, all free.
intro.start: Start on the bridge over the Aveyron, at the southern edge of the old town. From anywhere in the middle of town, walk down to the river and you will find it.

outro:
That is the six.

If you have any walking left, the pale cliff above the town is the Roc d'Anglars and there is a path up it. It is a stiff climb and it puts the whole town underneath you, roofs, river and all.

And if you are here on a Sunday morning, go back to the square. The market fills every street you have just walked down.

topics.name: The Water
topics.blurb: Two rivers meet here. Everything the town has ever done came out of that, including the worst day in its history.

topics.name: Knocked Down, Put Back
topics.blurb: An abbey, a ring of walls and a foreign garrison. Two of the three are gone.

topics.name: Still Standing
topics.blurb: The market and the oldest town hall in France, both still doing the job they were built for.

stops.title: The Bridge
stops.where: the road bridge over the Aveyron, at the southern edge of the old town

gate.prompt: Get onto the bridge, or onto the bank beside it, with the river in front of you.

stops.look:
Stand where you can see the water and the cliffs at the same time.

This is the Aveyron. A second, smaller river joins it here, the Bonnette. The pale rock wall standing over the town is the Roc d'Anglars.
stops.after:
The town owes its name to a body in a boat.

Antonin was killed at Pamiers, away to the south. The story goes that his corpse was put into a boat with nobody aboard, and that the boat came up this river steered by two white eagles and stopped here. A monastery went up on the spot in 763 and the town grew around it.

Noble Val is the rest of the name. The noble valley. Nobody was being modest.

The two rivers are the whole reason for the place. The Aveyron carried the trade. The Bonnette was small enough to be split into channels and put to work, and that is what made the tanners rich.

They flood as well. In March 1930 the water rose twelve or thirteen metres and put three quarters of the town under. You are going to stand in the middle of what it took.

stops.title: The Church That Is Younger Than It Looks
stops.where: the parish church of Saint-Antonin, on the square by the town hall
stops.directions:
Come off the bridge into the town and keep going straight ahead, away from the water, about a hundred and thirty metres.

You want the open square with the town hall on it and the church beside it. The church tower is the tallest thing in the middle of the town, so walk at that.

gate.prompt: Get to the square in front of the church, by the town hall.

stops.look:
Look at the church first, then look closely at the stone.

It is gothic. Pointed arches, tall windows, the lot. Now look at how regular the stonework is and how sharp every edge still is.
stops.after:
It was begun in 1862 and consecrated in 1872. It is younger than the railway.

The real one is gone. A Benedictine abbey was founded here in 763 and the town grew up around its walls. In 1562 the town, Protestant by then almost to a man, wrecked the abbey church, killed the canons and threw the Catholics out. It declared itself a Protestant republic and built its walls up higher.

That lasted sixty years. In June 1622 Louis XIII arrived with an army, took the town, and had the ramparts pulled down.

So a medieval walled town has no walls, and a town that grew up round an abbey has a Victorian church.

stops.title: Place du Bessarel
stops.where: Place du Bessarel, where the old canal runs through the town
stops.directions:
Leave the square on the far side from the bridge and work east through the narrow streets, downhill, towards the sound of running water. About a hundred and fifty metres.

You want an open square with a stone channel running through it, and a low open building standing over the water at one side.

question.hint: Look at the stone edge running along the water. It slopes down into it, and it has been worn smooth by something being rubbed on it.

stops.look:
The water going through here is not a river. It is a channel, cut on purpose, fed off the Bonnette.

At one side there is a low open building standing over it, with a long stone basin underneath and a sloping stone edge worn smooth.
stops.after:
Washing clothes. It is a lavoir, the village washhouse, and every French town of this size had one.

The channel is older than it looks. It was already being called the canal du Bessarel in 1315. This whole quarter ran on it. The tanners worked here, and the drapers, because turning hides into leather and washing raw wool both need running water, and neither is welcome upstream of where people drink.

Saint-Antonin got rich on leather in the 1200s and 1300s, calfskin above all, and sold it across the south of France.

Then the water took it back. The flood of March 1930 destroyed most of this quarter and two people drowned, one of them here. The square you are standing in only exists because of that. It was opened up afterwards, on the ground the flood had cleared.

One tannery is still standing.

stops.title: The Barracks on Guilhem Peyre
stops.where: rue Guilhem Peyre, one of the oldest streets in the town
stops.directions:
Head back west and uphill into the middle of the town, and find rue Guilhem Peyre. It is one of the narrow old streets running off the market square, and the name is on the wall at the corner.

Walk up it about a hundred and thirty metres, reading the fronts of the houses on both sides as you go.

question.ask: One house on this street was a barracks. Whose soldiers were in it?
question.hint: The house still carries the name, in French, on a plaque or over a door. It is the last word that matters.

stops.look:
Look along the house fronts for a name carved or painted on one of them, or a plaque set into the wall.

One of these buildings has been called the same thing for nearly seven hundred years, and the name says who was living in it.
stops.after:
The English. It is the Caserne des Anglais.

English troops were quartered here from 1352 to 1354, in the middle of the Hundred Years War, when this part of France was changing hands over and over. The house went on being a barracks long after they had gone, this time for the French crown.

They were here for two years. The name has lasted nearly seven centuries.

stops.title: The Covered Market
stops.where: the halle, in the main square in the middle of the town
stops.directions:
Walk straight back down rue Guilhem Peyre the way you came, about a hundred and thirty metres, until it opens out into the main square.

Go and stand underneath the covered market in the middle of it, in the shade.

gate.prompt: Get into the main square, under or beside the covered market.

stops.look:
Stand under the roof and look up at what is holding it there.

Then look round the square at the fronts of the buildings. One of them is a great deal older than the others.
stops.after:
The halle went up in 1841, and the people of the town paid for it themselves.

The market is still running. Sunday morning, seven until one, out of this square and up the streets around it. It is rated one of the best markets in Occitanie, which in this part of France is a serious claim.

This square also plays a French village in a film. The Hundred-Foot Journey was shot here over nine weeks in the autumn of 2013, with Helen Mirren running a restaurant and Om Puri running the rival one across the road. The scene where the pair of them go to the mayor to complain about each other was filmed on this square.

stops.title: The Oldest One
stops.where: the Maison Romane, the old consuls' house on the main square
stops.directions:
Come out from under the market roof and go straight across the square, about forty metres, to the tall stone building with the square tower on top.

Stand back far enough to take in the whole front of it, and to look up at the row of arches above the ground floor.

question.ask: Who are the two by the tree?
answers: adam and eve and the tree
adam and eve and the serpent
question.hint: Look at the row of small columns in the gallery above the big arches. The flat panels between them are carved. One has a tree with a figure standing on each side of it.

stops.look:
This is the oldest building on the walk and the small carvings are the point of it.

Look up at the gallery running above the big ground floor arches. Between the little columns there are flat carved panels with figures on them.

One panel has a man sitting down, holding a book. Another has two figures standing either side of a tree.
stops.after:
Adam and Eve, under the tree of knowledge.

The seated man with the book is the emperor Justinian, holding his book of laws. Putting those two together was not decoration. This building was a court. Justice was done in the hall behind those windows, so they carved the first crime and the first law code onto the front of it, where anybody waiting outside could see both.

The house went up around 1125 for the viscount of Saint-Antonin. It is generally called the oldest civil building in France. Not a church, not a castle. A town house. In 1312 the consuls bought it, and it was the town hall from then until the Revolution.

One warning. The square tower with the little loggia on top is not medieval. Viollet-le-Duc restored the building between 1846 and 1853 and the tower is his, invented whole. It is one of the more argued-about things he ever did, and it is the bit everybody photographs.

The carvings are the real ones. Nine hundred years old, high up on the front, and almost everybody walks straight past them.
